name: Chapter 12: Atoms
description: Thomson and Rutherford models, α-scattering, Bohr’s postulates, hydrogen energy levels and spectral series

cards.term: Thomson’s atom model (1898)?
cards.definition: Plum-pudding model: positive charge spread uniformly through the atom, with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon

cards.term: Why is Thomson’s model unstable?
cards.definition: Electrostatically unstable: charges cannot sit in stable equilibrium (Earnshaw). It also cannot give large-angle α-scattering

cards.term: Continuous vs line spectra: what emits which?
cards.definition: Hot solids, liquids and dense gases: continuous spectrum (interacting atoms). Rarefied excited gases: line spectrum from isolated atoms

cards.term: Why is a line spectrum called an atom’s “fingerprint”?
cards.definition: Each element emits a characteristic set of wavelengths with fixed relative positions, linked to its internal structure

cards.term: Balmer’s contribution (1885)?
cards.definition: An empirical formula for the wavelengths of a group of lines of atomic hydrogen

cards.term: Geiger–Marsden experiment (1911): source, target and detector?
cards.definition: 5.5 MeV α-particles from Bi-214 collimated by lead bricks hit a gold foil (2.1 × 10⁻⁷ m); scattered particles are seen as scintillations on a ZnS screen with a rotatable microscope

cards.term: Figure 12.2 · Geiger–Marsden set-up
Why is the experiment performed in a vacuum with a very thin foil?
cards.definition: Vacuum: no scattering by air. Thin foil: each α-particle suffers at most one scattering, so one nucleus explains each path

cards.term: Observations of the scattering experiment?
cards.definition: Most α-particles pass straight through ~0.14% scatter by more than 1° about 1 in 8000 deflect by more than 90°

cards.term: What did the results imply?
cards.definition: The atom is mostly empty space; all the positive charge and most of the mass sit in a tiny nucleus (10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹⁴ m vs atom 10⁻¹⁰ m)

cards.term: Ratio of atomic size to nuclear size?
cards.definition: About 10⁴ to 10⁵ (10⁻¹⁰ m / 10⁻¹⁴–10⁻¹⁵ m)

cards.term: Why do atomic electrons hardly affect α-particles?
cards.definition: They are 7300 times lighter than an α-particle; scattering comes from the massive nucleus

cards.term: Why is Rutherford credited with the discovery of the nucleus?
cards.definition: Backward deflection needs a large repulsive force: possible only if the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny centre

cards.term: Force on an α-particle at distance r from a nucleus of charge Ze?
cards.definition: \( F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{r^2} \) (Coulomb repulsion)

cards.term: Why can the gold nucleus be assumed stationary?
cards.definition: It is about 50 times heavier than an α-particle

cards.term: Define the impact parameter b.
cards.definition: The perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the α-particle from the centre of the nucleus

cards.term: Impact parameter and scattering angle?
cards.definition: Small b → large θ head-on (b ≈ 0) → θ ≈ 180° (rebound) large b → θ ≈ 0

cards.term: α-particle trajectories for different impact parameters
cards.definition: Small impact parameter gives large scattering angle; head-on gives nearly 180°; large b gives almost no deflection; the paths are hyperbolas; only about 1 in 8000 deflects beyond 90 degrees

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Rutherford scattering · trajectories

α-particles with different impact parameters b approach a gold nucleus. How does each one move?

Watch the path of each particle.

cards.term: Why do so few α-particles rebound?
cards.definition: Head-on collisions (very small b) are rare because the nucleus occupies a tiny area: it gives an upper limit on nuclear size

cards.term: Distance of closest approach in a head-on collision?
cards.definition: K = electrostatic PE at the turning point: \( \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{d} \), so \( d = \dfrac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K} \)

cards.term: Closest approach of a 7.7 MeV α-particle (Example 12.2)
cards.definition: d ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; the nucleus is smaller than this

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 12.2 · closest approach

Find the missing step.

A 7.7 MeV α-particle (K = 1.2 × 10⁻¹² J) is fired head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Find the distance of closest approach.
  1. At the turning point K = U: K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d
  2. d = 2Ze²/(4πε₀K) = (2 × 9 × 10⁹ × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)² Z)/(1.2 × 10⁻¹²)
  3. ?
  4. Z = 79: d ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 30 fm (upper bound; actual radius ≈ 6 fm)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 12.2 · closest approach

Find the missing step.

A 7.7 MeV α-particle (K = 1.2 × 10⁻¹² J) is fired head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Find the distance of closest approach.
  1. At the turning point K = U: K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d
  2. d = 2Ze²/(4πε₀K) = (2 × 9 × 10⁹ × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)² Z)/(1.2 × 10⁻¹²)
  3. d = 3.84 × 10⁻¹⁶ Z m
  4. Z = 79: d ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 30 fm (upper bound; actual radius ≈ 6 fm)

cards.term: Why does the closest-approach value exceed the actual gold nuclear radius (6 fm)?
cards.definition: The α-particle turns back without touching the nucleus: d is much larger than the sum of the radii (Coulomb repulsion acts at a distance)

cards.term: Teacher addition: how does the closest-approach distance depend on the energy K and charge Z?
cards.definition: d ∝ Z/K: doubling K halves d; a heavier nucleus (larger Z) repels more, so d is larger

cards.term: Teacher addition: Rutherford’s scattering formula?
cards.definition:
The number of α-particles scattered at angle θ per unit area: \( N \propto \dfrac{Z^2}{K^2\sin^4(\theta/2)} \).
So N ∝ Z², N ∝ 1/K², and it falls steeply with θ (Fig 12.3)

cards.term: Teacher addition: impact parameter and angle?
cards.definition: \( b = \dfrac{Ze^2\cot(\theta/2)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K} \): b → 0 as θ → 180°

cards.term: Teacher addition: why can’t Thomson’s model explain 1 in 8000 backward scattering?
cards.definition: With charge spread over 10⁻¹⁰ m the field is weak, so the maximum deflection of a heavy, fast α-particle is tiny (< 0.01°); many small deflections never add up to 90°

cards.term: Example 12.1: if the solar system had the atom’s proportions (orbit/nucleus = 10⁵), how far would Earth be from the Sun?
cards.definition: Sun’s radius 7 × 10⁸ m × 10⁵ = 7 × 10¹³ m, more than 100 times the real 1.5 × 10¹¹ m: the atom is far emptier than the solar system

cards.term: Condition for a stable circular orbit of the electron in hydrogen (Rutherford model)?
cards.definition: Coulomb force = centripetal force: \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \), so \( r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 mv^2} \)

cards.term: Kinetic, potential and total energy of the electron in a hydrogen orbit of radius r?
cards.definition: \( K = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r},\ U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r},\ E = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r} \)

cards.term: Ratio K : U : E for a hydrogen orbit? Why is E negative?
cards.definition: K : U : E = 1 : −2 : −1, so E = −K = U/2. Negative E means the electron is bound; E > 0 would give an open (unbound) path

cards.term: Teacher addition: what happens to K, U and E when an electron moves to a larger orbit?
cards.definition: K falls, U rises (less negative), E rises (less negative): the atom absorbs energy

cards.term: Bohr radius from the ionisation energy (Example 12.3)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 12.3 · radius and speed

Find the missing step.

13.6 eV separates a hydrogen atom into a proton and an electron. Find the orbital radius and the electron’s speed.
  1. E = −13.6 eV = −2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = −e²/(8πε₀r)
  2. ?
  3. v = e/√(4πε₀ m r)
  4. v ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 12.3 · radius and speed

Find the missing step.

13.6 eV separates a hydrogen atom into a proton and an electron. Find the orbital radius and the electron’s speed.
  1. E = −13.6 eV = −2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = −e²/(8πε₀r)
  2. r = e²/(8πε₀|E|) = (9 × 10⁹)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(2 × 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m
  3. v = e/√(4πε₀ m r)
  4. v ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s

cards.term: Emission line spectrum: definition?
cards.definition: Bright lines on a dark background from an excited rarefied gas at low pressure, each line at a specific wavelength (the “fingerprint” of the element)

cards.term: Absorption spectrum?
cards.definition: Dark lines in a continuous spectrum seen when white light passes through a gas: the dark lines fall at exactly the same wavelengths as the emission lines of that gas

cards.term: Kirchhoff/Fraunhofer application?
cards.definition: Dark lines in sunlight (Fraunhofer lines) reveal the elements in the Sun’s atmosphere (helium was found this way)

cards.term: Two failures of Rutherford’s planetary model (classical physics)?
cards.definition: (1) An orbiting (accelerating) electron radiates and would spiral into the nucleus: atoms unstable. (2) Frequency of emitted light would change continuously: continuous spectrum, not lines

cards.term: Example 12.4: classical frequency of light from the H electron at r = 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m, v = 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s?
cards.definition: ν = v/2πr = 6.6 × 10¹⁵ Hz

cards.term: Print note: Example 12.4 writes the electron speed as 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ m/s in words. Right?
cards.definition: Typo (printed in the sentence): it is 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s, as the formula next to it uses

cards.term: Bohr’s first postulate?
cards.definition: The electron can revolve in certain stable (stationary) orbits without radiating, each with a definite energy

cards.term: Bohr’s second postulate (quantum condition)?
cards.definition: Angular momentum is quantised: \( L = mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi},\ n = 1, 2, 3, \dots \)

cards.term: Bohr’s third postulate?
cards.definition:
The electron may jump to a lower-energy orbit and emit a photon: \( h\nu = E_i - E_f \).
Absorbing a photon of the same energy lifts it back

cards.term: Radius of the nth Bohr orbit?
cards.definition: \( r_n = \dfrac{n^2h^2\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^2} = n^2 a_0 \), a₀ = 0.529 Å (Bohr radius); r ∝ n²

cards.term: Energy of the nth level of hydrogen?
cards.definition: \( E_n = -\dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^2n^2} = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \) with E₁ = −13.6 eV. In joules: −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J

cards.term: Teacher addition: speed of the electron in the nth orbit?
cards.definition: \( v_n = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0 nh} = \dfrac{2.19\times10^6}{n}\ m/s \) (v ∝ 1/n)

cards.term: Teacher addition: scaling with n: r, v, E, T, K, L?
cards.definition: r ∝ n² v ∝ 1/n E, K, |U| ∝ 1/n² time period T ∝ n³ frequency of revolution ∝ 1/n³ angular momentum ∝ n

cards.term: Teacher addition: hydrogen-like ions (He⁺, Li²⁺) with atomic number Z?
cards.definition:
r_n = n²a₀/Z
v_n = Zv₁/n
\( E_n = -\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2} \) eV (Bohr model works for any one-electron ion)

cards.term: Ionisation energy of hydrogen? Excitation energies?
cards.definition: Ionisation: 13.6 eV from n = 1. To n = 2: 10.2 eV; to n = 3: 12.09 eV

cards.term: Ground state and excited states?
cards.definition: Ground state: n = 1, E = −13.6 eV, orbit of radius a₀. Excited states: n > 1. Higher n means higher (less negative) energy

cards.term: Figure 12.7 · Hydrogen energy levels
Figure 12.7 · Energy values (eV)
What does E = 0 at n = ∞ mean? What about E > 0?
cards.definition: The electron is completely removed and at rest. Above 0 the electron is free with a continuum of energies

cards.term: How do the level spacings vary with n?
cards.definition: Energies come closer together as n increases (E ∝ 1/n²)

cards.term: As n increases, what happens to the energy needed to free the electron?
cards.definition: It decreases (binding energy = 13.6/n² eV)

cards.term: At room temperature where are most hydrogen atoms?
cards.definition: In the ground state (n = 1); excitation needs collisions or photon absorption

cards.term: Intuition: why do the levels crowd together near E = 0?
cards.definition: E = −13.6/n²: successive gaps 13.6(1/n² − 1/(n+1)²) shrink as ~ 27/n³, so high levels merge into the ionisation continuum

cards.term: Frequency of the photon emitted in a jump from n_i to n_f?
cards.definition: \( h\nu = E_{n_i} - E_{n_f} = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}\right) \) eV

cards.term: Rydberg formula for the wavelength?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}\right) \), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (Rydberg constant)

cards.term: Why is the spectrum discrete?
cards.definition: Only certain n exist, so ΔE takes discrete values, giving discrete frequencies

cards.term: Absorption in Bohr’s model?
cards.definition: A photon whose energy exactly equals E_f − E_i lifts the electron up: dark absorption lines appear at the same frequencies as emission lines

cards.term: Figure 12.5 · Hydrogen spectral series
Hydrogen spectral series (teacher addition table)
cards.definition: Lyman: n_f = 1; ultraviolet; limit 91.2 nm (122 nm to 91 nm); Balmer: n_f = 2; visible (and near UV); 656.3 nm (Hα) to limit 364.6 nm; Paschen: n_f = 3; infrared; 1875 nm to limit 820 nm; Brackett: n_f = 4; infrared (far); Pfund: n_f = 5; infrared (far)

cards.term: Mnemonic: order of the hydrogen series (n_f = 1 → 5)?
cards.definition: “Little Boys Play Ball Practice”: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (UV, visible, then infrared ×3)

cards.term: Teacher addition: wavelengths of the first Balmer lines (n = 3, 4, 5, 6 → 2)?
cards.definition: 656 nm (red, Hα), 486 nm (blue-green), 434 nm (violet), 410 nm (violet)

cards.term: Teacher addition: longest and shortest wavelengths of a series?
cards.definition: Longest: jump from n_f + 1 to n_f (first line). Shortest: from ∞ (series limit), 1/λ = R/n_f². Lyman limit 91.2 nm; Balmer limit 364.6 nm

cards.term: Teacher addition: maximum number of spectral lines from an electron that starts in level n?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \) (all possible drops between levels): n = 4 gives 6 lines

cards.term: Teacher addition: for the same Δn, which transitions give the largest photon energy?
cards.definition: Transitions ending at n = 1 (Lyman): energy gaps are biggest near the nucleus

cards.term: Teacher addition: what is “the third line of the Balmer series”?
cards.definition: n = 5 → 2 (434 nm): the first line is 3 → 2, second 4 → 2, third 5 → 2

cards.term: Photon absorbed for 1 → 4 (Exercise 12.5)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 12.5 · absorbing to n = 4

Find the missing step.

A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a photon and jumps to n = 4. Find the photon’s wavelength and frequency.
  1. ?
  2. ΔE = 12.75 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.04 × 10⁻¹⁸ J
  3. ν = ΔE/h = 3.1 × 10¹⁵ Hz
  4. λ = c/ν = 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ m (97 nm, UV)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 12.5 · absorbing to n = 4

Find the missing step.

A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a photon and jumps to n = 4. Find the photon’s wavelength and frequency.
  1. ΔE = 13.6 (1/1² − 1/4²) = 12.75 eV
  2. ΔE = 12.75 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.04 × 10⁻¹⁸ J
  3. ν = ΔE/h = 3.1 × 10¹⁵ Hz
  4. λ = c/ν = 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ m (97 nm, UV)

cards.term: De Broglie’s explanation of Bohr’s quantisation (1923)?
cards.definition: The electron orbit must hold a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: 2πr_n = nλ (a circular standing wave)

cards.term: Derive L = nh/2π from the standing wave.
cards.definition: 2πr = nλ with λ = h/mv gives 2πr = nh/mv, so mvr = nh/2π

cards.term: Who verified the wave nature of electrons and when?
cards.definition: Davisson and Germer (1927)

cards.term: What happens to wavelengths that do not fit the orbit?
cards.definition: They interfere destructively with themselves after each turn and their amplitude dies out; only resonant standing waves survive

cards.term: Teacher addition: de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the nth orbit?
cards.definition: \( \lambda_n = \dfrac{h}{mv_n} = \dfrac{2\pi r_n}{n} \), so n wavelengths fit the nth orbit

cards.term: Limitations of Bohr’s model?
cards.definition: (i) Works only for hydrogenic (one-electron) atoms, not even helium (electron–electron forces ignored). (ii) Cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines

cards.term: Hydrogenic atoms: definition and examples?
cards.definition: A nucleus of charge +Ze with a single electron: H, He⁺, Li²⁺…

cards.term: Why can’t Bohr’s planet-like model be applied to many-electron atoms?
cards.definition: Electron–electron repulsion is comparable to nucleus–electron attraction (unlike planet–planet forces compared to the Sun’s pull)

cards.term: Other limitations exams mention?
cards.definition: Inconsistent with the uncertainty principle (fixed orbits with definite r and p); does not explain fine structure, Zeeman effect, or chemical bonding

cards.term: Why study Bohr’s model still?
cards.definition: Three simple postulates explain the main features of the hydrogen spectrum, use classical concepts, and show how physicists build models and test them

cards.term: Modern picture of Bohr orbits?
cards.definition: In quantum mechanics they become regions of high probability of finding the electron; a state needs four quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) but for hydrogen E depends only on n

cards.term: Why did Bohr quantise angular momentum specifically?
cards.definition: h has the dimensions of angular momentum, and angular momentum is the natural quantity for circular orbits

cards.term: Frequency of revolution vs frequency of the spectral line?
cards.definition: Not equal in Bohr’s model (line frequency = ΔE/h); they coincide only for large n (n → n − 1), the correspondence principle

cards.term: NEET pattern: ratio of the shortest wavelength of Balmer to Lyman series?
cards.definition: Balmer limit: 1/λ_B = R/4; Lyman limit: 1/λ_L = R. So λ_B/λ_L = 4 : 1

cards.term: NEET pattern: ratio of the longest wavelengths of the Lyman and Balmer series?
cards.definition: Lyman: 1/λ = R(1 − 1/4) = 3R/4. Balmer: R(1/4 − 1/9) = 5R/36. Ratio λ_L : λ_B = (4/3R) : (36/5R) = 5 : 27

cards.term: JEE pattern: an electron in the n = 3 state of H⁻like He⁺ (Z = 2). Its energy and radius vs hydrogen n = 3?
cards.definition: E = −13.6 × 4/9 = −6.04 eV (4× more negative); radius = 9a₀/2 = 4.5 a₀ (half)

cards.term: JEE pattern: hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a 12.75 eV photon. Which lines appear on de-excitation?
cards.definition: Goes to n = 4; possible lines = 4 × 3/2 = 6: 3 Lyman, 2 Balmer, 1 Paschen

cards.term: JEE pattern: minimum energy photon that can ionise a hydrogen atom in the n = 2 state?
cards.definition: 3.4 eV (binding energy 13.6/4)

cards.term: Pattern: a 12.5 eV electron beam bombards hydrogen. Which series can be excited?
cards.definition:
Highest reachable n satisfies 13.6(1 − 1/n²) ≤ 12.5 → n = 3 (12.09 eV): Lyman (122, 103 nm) and Balmer (656 nm).
No Paschen lines (Exercise 12.8)

cards.term: Pattern: kinetic energy of the electron in the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen?
cards.definition: K = −E = 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV, PE = −6.8 eV

cards.term: Pattern: angular momentum of the electron in the third orbit?
cards.definition: L = 3h/2π = 3.16 × 10⁻³⁴ J s

cards.term: Board pattern: state Bohr’s postulates and derive the radius of the nth orbit (outline)?
cards.definition:
Coulomb = centripetal: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²).
With mvr = nh/2π eliminate v: \( r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m e^2} \)

cards.term: Board pattern: two limitations of Rutherford’s model?
cards.definition: Atoms would be unstable (radiating electron spirals in) and would emit a continuous rather than a line spectrum

cards.term: Why are both Thomson’s and Rutherford’s models unstable?
cards.definition: Thomson’s: electrostatically unstable. Rutherford’s: unstable due to radiation by the orbiting electron

cards.term: What did the uncertainty principle do to Bohr’s orbits?
cards.definition: The exact orbit picture is inconsistent with it; orbits become probability regions in quantum mechanics

cards.term:
Exercise 12.1: complete:
(a) The size of the atom in Thomson’s model is ___ the atomic size in Rutherford’s.
(b) Ground-state stable equilibrium in ___, net force always in ___.
(c) A classical atom based on ___ collapses.
(d) Nearly continuous mass in ___, highly non-uniform in ___.
(e) Positive part has most of the mass in ___.
cards.definition: (a) no different from. (b) Thomson’s model; Rutherford’s model. (c) Rutherford’s model. (d) Thomson’s; Rutherford’s. (e) both models

cards.term: Exercise 12.2: repeat the α-scattering with solid hydrogen foil instead of gold. What results?
cards.definition: A proton is lighter than the α-particle (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ vs 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg), so the α-particle cannot bounce back (like a football hitting a tennis ball): no large-angle scattering; the protons are knocked forward

cards.term: Exercise 12.3: two levels 2.3 eV apart. Frequency of the emitted radiation?
cards.definition: ν = ΔE/h = 2.3 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz

cards.term: Exercise 12.4: ground state of hydrogen is −13.6 eV. KE and PE of the electron?
cards.definition: K = −E = +13.6 eV; U = 2E = −27.2 eV

cards.term: Bohr speeds and periods (Exercise 12.6)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 12.6 · speeds and periods

Find the missing step.

Bohr model: speed of the electron in hydrogen for n = 1, 2, 3 and the orbital period in each.
  1. v_n = v₁/n with v₁ = 2.18 × 10⁶ m/s
  2. v = 2.18 × 10⁶, 1.09 × 10⁶, 7.27 × 10⁵ m/s
  3. r_n = n² × 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m; T = 2πr/v
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 12.6 · speeds and periods

Find the missing step.

Bohr model: speed of the electron in hydrogen for n = 1, 2, 3 and the orbital period in each.
  1. v_n = v₁/n with v₁ = 2.18 × 10⁶ m/s
  2. v = 2.18 × 10⁶, 1.09 × 10⁶, 7.27 × 10⁵ m/s
  3. r_n = n² × 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m; T = 2πr/v
  4. T = 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁶ s, 1.22 × 10⁻¹⁵ s, 4.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ s (T ∝ n³)

cards.term: Exercise 12.7: radius of the n = 1 orbit is 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Radii for n = 2 and 3?
cards.definition: r ∝ n²: 2.12 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and 4.77 × 10⁻¹⁰ m

cards.term: Exercise 12.8: 12.5 eV electrons bombard hydrogen at room temperature. Series of wavelengths emitted?
cards.definition: Highest level reached is n = 3 (12.09 eV). Lyman: 103 nm and 122 nm; Balmer: 656 nm

cards.term: Exercise 12.9: quantum number of Earth’s orbit (r = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m, v = 3 × 10⁴ m/s, M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg)?
cards.definition: n = mvr/(h/2π) = (6 × 10²⁴ × 3 × 10⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹¹)/(1.055 × 10⁻³⁴) = 2.6 × 10⁷⁴ (so quantisation is invisible for macroscopic bodies)

cards.term: Chapter 12 formula sheet
cards.definition: Distance of closest approach: d = 2Ze²/(4πε₀K); Orbit energy (classical): K = −E, U = 2E; Bohr quantisation: mvr = nh/2π; Bohr radius: r_n = n² × 0.529 Å; Energy levels: E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV; Photon emitted: hν = E_i − E_f; Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²); de Broglie orbits: 2πr_n = nλ

cards.term: Chapter 12 concept checks
cards.definition: Most α-particles are scattered by more than 90°: False (about 1 in 8000); Bohr’s model works for helium atom (two electrons): False; Energy of the hydrogen electron is negative in every bound state: True; Balmer series lies entirely in the infrared: False (visible/near UV); Lyman series transitions end at n = 1: True; Bohr’s model explains the relative intensities of lines: False

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Concept checks

True or false?

Most α-particles are scattered by more than 90°?
